Hi George,

Good job on resolving the issue yourself, I would like to share here the correct procedure to install/uninstall MRO and MKL for future reference.

Uninstallation:
First, uninstall MKL Math Libraries. This will revert to the original Rblas.dll and Rlapack.dll files.
Remove the RevoMath package using the Windows instructions for uninstalling a program specific to your version of Windows. For example, on Windows 8.1, choose Control Panel > Programs & Features > Uninstall.

Find RevoMath in the list and uninstall.
Then, uninstall Microsoft R Open :

Remove Microsoft R Open using the Windows instructions for uninstalling a program specific to your version of Windows. For example, on Windows 8, choose Control Panel > Programs & Features > Uninstall.

Find MRO for Windows 3.2.3 in the list and uninstall.

Remove the directory in which you installed Microsoft R Open, by default C:\Program Files\MicrosoftMRO.

Installation:
Launch the Microsoft R Open installer and follow the prompts.
After installing Microsoft R Open, you can enable the optional multi-threaded performance for Microsoft R Open as follows:
Warning!  Install Microsoft R Open first before MKL. If you reinstall Microsoft R Open without removing MKL, your MKL will no longer work. Instead, you must first uninstall MKL first as described above

A. Download <https://mran.microsoft.com/download/#download> the Math Kernel Library (MKL) corresponding for this release of Microsoft R Open.

B. Go to the directory into which you downloaded RevoMath-3.2.3.exe, the MKL utility.

C. Launch the installer and follow the prompts.

Thanks,

Smit

1. Creating a personal library

It's not clear to me why R doesn't create your personal library folder, so I suggest you create this manually.

To do this, create a folder C:/Users/<<USERNAME>>/Documents/R/win-library/3.2

(Remember to substitute your own windows user name for <<YOURNAME>>

Then your package installation should work.

2. There is no inherent reason why all packages won't work with R Open.  I know of one or two exceptions where a package did not play well with the Intel MKL, but we try to work with the package authors when we discover issues like this. Bu this is highly exceptional - I literally know only of two cases where this has ever happened.

3. How to install all packages from a repository was answered at http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2169118/installing-all-cran-packages-that-are-not-already-installed

However, you'll have to modify the code to point to BioConductor:

BioC <- "http://bioconductor.org/packages/3.0/bioc"
available.packages(contriburl = contrib.url(BioC))

--

I hope this helps.

Andrie

messages.body_plain:
I've an interesting challenge to speed up my code in the simplest way possible.  I'm looping through hundreds/thousands of time series and performing rolling origin forecasting on each time series.  So this means multiple origins, multiple time series and multiple forecasting methods (eg exponential smoothing, ARIMA, stepwise regression, etc.)

Currently I'm making use of the cores available to me and multi-threading via the foreach package so I can run 8 simultaneous time series at a time (16 in parallel on the university cluster, potentially many more if I use multiple nodes).  My questions are related to speeding up the task:

1) would moving from out-of-the-box R to MRO be of benefit to me?  Is this because the MKL extensions make the calculations perform faster on a SINGLE core or because MKL enables parallel use of the cores?  I imagine some code profiling would be required to highlight exactly where my code is running slowest (e.g. solve, optim, lm)

2) I have access to a cluster where Intel Xeon Phis (MICs) are available.  Would the foreach package play nicely with the MIC or would it struggle with running 240 instances of R in parallel?  Does MRO play nicely with the MIC co-processor?  Do you have any case studies or documentation of using the MIC to run more simultaneous threads on MRO?

Any other suggestions you would make to advise me on optimisation of this code?

Many thanks in advance,

Matt

messages.subject_clean: Speeding up my code
messages.body_plain:
Interesting question.

The Intel MKL will speed up any BLAS operations, e.g. matrix multiplication, cholesky decomposition, etc. So solve() might run faster, but optim() probably won't (depending on what you're trying to optimise). One would think that lm() also falls into this category, but the lm() code does not call out to any BLAS functions, so it will be the same speed.

The foreach package does not have a parallel backend for Xeon Phi, as far as I know.

However, the MKL does support Xeon Phi, as this blog post explains: http://blog.revolutionanalytics.com/2015/05/behold-the-power-of-parallel.html, but beware, the author effectively says "here be dragons".

I hope this helps.

Good luck with your project!

Andrie

Improvements include long-vector support for the smooth function, a newstringsAsFactors options when using rbind with data frames, and better rounding from the summary function in the presence of some infinite values.

This release uses a CRAN snapshot taken on April 1, 2016 as the default package repository. Many packages have been updated since the release of MRO 3.2.3, including implementations of the Bayesian bootstrap <https://mran.microsoft.com/package/bayesboot/>, deep boosting <https://mran.microsoft.com/package/deepboost/>, multivariate <https://mran.microsoft.com/package/MultivariateRandomForest/> and fuzzy random forests <https://mran.microsoft.com/package/fuzzyforest/>, and balanced sampling <https://mran.microsoft.com/package/BalancedSampling/>. There's a summary of package changes provided in the package spotlight for Microsoft R Open 3.2.4 <https://mran.microsoft.com/spotlight/#mro324-repos-pkgs>. To download Microsoft R Open 3.2.4, visit MRAN at the link below.
